row.basis: watering furrows; soil softened for grain
row.note: The commentary begins with rain squeezed from clouds and later with crops; this psalm has God water the furrows and prepare grain, joining rainfall directly to yield.

row.basis: early rain and latter rain
row.note: The commentary links rain to plants that grow after it; Joel's restoration promise names seasonal rains as the setting for renewed agricultural abundance.

row.basis: threshing floor full
row.note: After Joel's rain promise, this verse says the threshing floors fill with grain and vats overflow, giving the same rain-to-harvest sequence the commentary draws from cloud to crop.

row.basis: rain makes earth sprout and yield seed and bread
row.note: The commentary moves from rain to plant growth and harvest; Isaiah's rain and snow water the earth so it sprouts, supplying seed for sowing and bread for food, a closely matched growth sequence.

row.basis: grass for cattle; plants for people
row.note: The commentary says pasture gives itself to the herd and describes grain as human yield; this verse pairs God-grown grass for cattle with plants for human use.

row.basis: pastures with flocks; valleys with grain
row.note: The commentary connects rain-fed pasture and harvested grain; this verse places flocks in pasture and grain in valleys in one picture of a fruitful landscape.

row.basis: fat cows grazing beside lean cows
row.note: The commentary's camel fattens on spring growth; Pharaoh's dream makes fat, grazing cows the sign of abundant years, with their lean counterparts marking the coming reversal.

row.basis: green pasture and still waters
row.note: The commentary describes pasture nourishing a herd; the shepherd here leads the speaker to green pasture and water, adding a personal image of provision that prevents want.

row.basis: tree beside water; fruit in season
row.note: The commentary pictures the exception to loss as plants joined in unbroken greenery; Psalm 1's planted tree bears fruit at its time and its leaf does not wither, giving that flourishing a righteous figure.

row.basis: chaff driven by wind
row.note: The commentary's whirlwind lifts dust and its crop image ends in disappearance; Psalm 1 contrasts its fruiting tree with the wicked as wind-scattered chaff.

row.basis: watered tree endures heat and drought
row.note: The commentary's connected greenery stands against the lost harvest; Jeremiah's tree by water stays green in heat and continues bearing fruit even in drought, a specific image of endurance.

row.basis: fruit in old age; fresh and green
row.note: The commentary says a life's accumulated crop can be lost in its late years; this psalm instead says the righteous still bear fruit in old age, explicitly reversing that late-life outcome.

row.basis: עצר; rain restrained (table sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary's ع ص ر image releases rain from a pressed cloud; the package's table gives Hebrew עצר as a sound correspondence, and this verse uses it for heaven being restrained so rain and land-yield cease.

row.basis: חשר; collection of watery clouds (table notes BDB's Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary develops rain-bearing and layered clouds, while the package's חשר entry describes a gathering of watery clouds and notes an Arabic cognate; Job's context concerns the spread of clouds, so the lexical link is suggestive but uncertain.

row.basis: חסר; lack (table sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary labels خسر as the loss of a harvest; the package lists חסר as a corresponding Hebrew root, and the shepherd-speaker says he will not lack, giving a concrete opposite outcome under care.

row.basis: מחסור; lack of everything (table sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary glosses خسر as a crop's disappearance; the package's חסר correspondence appears here in a covenant curse of hunger, thirst, nakedness, and total lack, making the loss material and collective.

row.basis: צבר; grain heaped up (table sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary gives صبرة as food piled upon food; the package lists צבר as a sound correspondence, and Genesis uses it for Joseph's immense heaping of grain, matching the concrete heap sense.

row.basis: חק; a prescribed share of produce (table sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary calls the crop's due on harvest day its حق; the package's חקק correspondence means something prescribed, and Genesis fixes a fifth of the land's yield as a statute, making the crop's allotted share concrete.

row.basis: forgotten sheaf left for the vulnerable
row.note: The commentary says the crop has a due on harvest day; this law leaves a forgotten sheaf for the immigrant, orphan, and widow, showing harvested produce as a social obligation.

row.basis: sowing much, gathering little to locusts
row.note: The commentary's central loss image is a vanished harvest; this curse has abundant sowing yield little because locusts consume it, specifying one way the crop is lost.

row.basis: produce worked for but not enjoyed
row.note: The commentary says a lifetime's yield can disappear; Micah names sowing without reaping, olives without oil, and grapes without wine, turning that loss into denied agricultural labor.

row.basis: sow righteousness; reap steadfast love; rain righteousness
row.note: The commentary joins good deeds and mutual counsel to its green-growth image; Hosea commands sowing righteousness and seeking God until rain comes, linking ethical action to a promised harvest.

row.basis: sowing in tears, reaping in joy
row.note: The commentary pairs steadfastness with the crop's rise and loss; this psalm makes a painful sowing issue in joyful reaping, adding a hope-filled harvest after hardship.

row.basis: sow morning and evening without slackening
row.note: The commentary's exception holds to patient good work; Ecclesiastes tells the sower not to rest because the successful yield is unknown, giving patience an agricultural practice.

row.basis: grass and flower wither when wind blows
row.note: The commentary's cyclone lifts dust and destroys the crop; Isaiah says grass withers when the divine breath blows and identifies people with grass, bringing human transience into the weather image.

row.basis: tumbleweed and chaff before wind
row.note: The commentary describes a whirlwind lifting dust into a column; this verse makes enemies like rolling dust and wind-driven chaff, using airborne scattering as an image of defeat.

row.basis: fire consuming forest
row.note: The commentary's fiery cyclone burns a garden; this verse compares judgment on enemies to fire consuming a forest, extending the storm image to vegetation destroyed by flame.

row.basis: storm and tempest pursuing enemies
row.note: The commentary's إعصار is a destructive wind column; this verse calls for enemies to be pursued by storm and tempest, using violent weather as an image of reversal and judgment.

row.basis: continue the work without needing to finish it
row.note: The commentary's righteous community keeps urging patience while doing good; this maxim says one need not complete the work but is not free to desist, adding persistence when a lifetime may not see the yield.

row.basis: stalk, head, then full grain
row.note: The commentary says the grain is named عصر when its husk appears and then describes its yield; Mark's seed parable traces growth through stalk, head, and full grain, closely matching that crop-stage sequence.

row.basis: sickle when the harvest is ready
row.note: The commentary moves from grain's formation to its yield; Mark ends the growing sequence with the sickle at harvest, supplying the moment when the crop becomes gathered produce.

row.basis: fruit borne with endurance
row.note: The commentary joins good deeds and patience to its crop imagery; Luke's good-soil hearers hold fast and bear fruit with endurance, directly linking ethical reception to patient yield.

row.basis: farmer waits for fruit and early and late rain
row.note: The commentary connects rain-fed growth with patience; James tells believers to wait like a farmer for the earth's precious fruit through the rains, adding patient expectation to the crop image.

row.basis: community told to be patient and strengthen hearts
row.note: The commentary says the righteous mutually urge one another to patience; James addresses the community and tells them to be patient and steady-hearted as the Lord's coming draws near.

row.basis: doing good reaped in due season
row.note: The commentary links righteous action and patience; Paul says not to tire of doing good because the harvest comes at its season if they do not give up, making the ethical crop analogy explicit.

row.basis: rained land produces useful vegetation
row.note: The commentary's cloud gives rain and the exception is a green, productive community; Hebrews compares hearers to land that drinks frequent rain and produces useful vegetation, interpreting response as fruitful growth.

row.basis: thorns, curse, and burning
row.note: The commentary's storm can burn an entire garden; Hebrews contrasts productive land with ground bearing thorns and thistles, near a curse and destined for burning.

row.basis: vine and branches bear fruit by remaining joined
row.note: The commentary says those excepted from loss interconnect like continuous greenery; Jesus depicts branches joined to a vine and bearing much fruit by abiding, giving the joined-plant image a communal source of fruitfulness.

row.basis: severed branch withers and is burned
row.note: The commentary's crop can be destroyed by a fiery whirlwind; Jesus says the branch that does not abide withers, is gathered, and burned, joining disconnection, loss, and fire.

row.basis: truth spoken as the body grows
row.note: The commentary's people mutually counsel one another to truth; Ephesians joins speaking truth with growing into Christ, adding growth as the outcome of truthful communal practice.

row.basis: joined body grows as each part works
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel into plants connected as one green pasture; Ephesians describes a body joined together with every part working so it grows and builds itself up, a specific social counterpart to interconnected growth.

row.basis: admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all
row.note: The commentary's exception consists of people who urge one another to truth and patience; Paul specifies communal admonition, encouragement of the fainthearted, help for the weak, and patience toward all.

row.basis: rain and wind strike a house founded on rock, but it stands
row.note: The commentary pairs a destructive storm with hard stone; Jesus' house withstands rain, flood, and wind because it is founded on rock, making stability the opposite outcome of the ruined garden.

row.basis: grain dies and bears much fruit
row.note: The commentary's late-life storm destroys a life's yield; Jesus says a grain of wheat that dies produces much fruit, turning the death of a seed into multiplication rather than loss.

row.basis: work burned and its maker suffers loss, yet is saved
row.note: The commentary likens failed works to ash blown away; Paul says a person's work may be burned and suffer loss while the person is saved, distinguishing lost product from lost person.

row.basis: abundant crops stored in larger barns
row.note: The commentary's harvest can represent a life's accumulated product; the rich man plans larger barns for his abundant produce, making stored yield the object later put at risk.

row.basis: life required before stored goods can be used
row.note: The commentary says the storm may destroy the whole accumulation late in life; the rich man is told that his life is required that night and is asked who will own his stored goods, making the harvest's futility personal.

row.basis: water bound in clouds; cloud holds its burden
row.note: The commentary's cloud is compressed with rain before releasing it; Job depicts God binding water in clouds without their bursting, adding a precise image of cloud containment.

row.basis: small cloud rising from the sea
row.note: The commentary develops rain-bearing clouds; Elijah's servant sees a cloud rising from the sea, a specific cloud sign that precedes the rain.

row.basis: sky blackens and heavy rain begins
row.note: The commentary moves from a rain cloud to the water it releases; after the small cloud, this verse describes darkening skies and heavy rain, completing that weather sequence.

row.basis: rain sent where no person lives
row.note: The commentary pictures rain delivered to a community; Job asks about rain given to an uninhabited land, adding the counterpoint that rain also serves places without human recipients.

row.basis: wilderness satisfied; grass sprouts
row.note: The commentary links rain with greening plants; Job's next verse says the desolate land is satisfied and tender grass sprouts, spelling out the water-to-growth result.

row.basis: storm clouds, showers, and field grass
row.note: The commentary links a rain cloud to pasture growth; Zechariah asks for rain from the maker of storm clouds, which gives showers and field grass.

row.basis: riverside trees fruit every month; leaves do not wither
row.note: The commentary's exception is continuous interconnected greenery; Ezekiel's riverbank trees never fail to fruit and keep healing leaves, extending the image to perennial abundance.

row.basis: feed the hungry and satisfy the afflicted
row.note: The commentary assigns the harvest a due and makes righteous action part of its green community; Isaiah makes feeding the hungry the condition of the promised light and renewal that follows.

row.basis: watered garden and unfailing spring
row.note: The commentary joins righteous practice to a rain-fed green world; Isaiah promises that the person who acts for the hungry will be like a watered garden whose spring does not fail.

row.basis: honor God with firstfruits
row.note: The commentary says the crop has a due on harvest day; Proverbs gives the first produce to honor God, making the yield a prescribed offering.

row.basis: full barns and overflowing vats
row.note: The commentary traces rain through crop to gathered produce; Proverbs depicts full barns and overflowing wine vats as the result of honoring God with firstfruits.

row.basis: first produce placed in a basket
row.note: The commentary names the crop's due on harvest day; Deuteronomy requires the first of the land's produce to be gathered in a basket, giving that due a ritual form.

row.basis: firstfruits presented before God
row.note: The commentary connects harvest to an owed share; this verse has the worshipper present the firstfruits as an offering, making the harvest's claim a liturgical act.

row.basis: rejoice with Levite and immigrant
row.note: The commentary makes fruitful life a shared community image; the firstfruits rite culminates in rejoicing with the Levite and immigrant, extending the crop's benefit beyond its grower.

row.basis: threshing ox allowed to eat grain
row.note: The commentary says pasture gives itself to the herd and the harvest has a due; this law lets the working ox eat from the grain it threshes, assigning a share of produce to the animal laborer.

row.basis: עצר; festival assembly (table's sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary describes rain falling on a community; the package's table pairs Arabic ع ص ر with Hebrew עצר and lists festival assembly as a Hebrew use, while Leviticus names an assembly at the ingathering festival. This is a lexical and communal echo, not proof of cognacy.

row.basis: sowing wind, reaping whirlwind; stalk without a head yields no flour
row.note: The commentary's cyclone raises dust and its lost harvest disappears; Hosea binds whirlwind to failed grain, explicitly saying the stalk has no head and yields no flour.

row.basis: great wind collapses a house and kills the children inside
row.note: The commentary's fiery storm destroys a garden while its owner has weak children; Job's wind destroys a household and its children, adding the family cost of a sudden storm, though the objects and cause differ.

row.basis: flour and oil do not run out during drought
row.note: The commentary presents the harvest as lost; during a drought, the widow's flour and oil remain sufficient, a specific counterexample of provision continuing without a new crop.

row.basis: sowing to flesh reaps corruption; sowing to Spirit reaps life
row.note: The commentary says humanity is in loss except those who do good; Paul assigns contrasting harvests to two ways of life, making the ethical distinction a direct sowing-and-reaping contrast.

row.basis: seed scattered on the ground
row.note: The commentary follows rain through plant growth to harvest; Jesus begins a kingdom parable with a person scattering seed, adding the human act that starts the growth sequence.

row.basis: seed grows while the sower does not know how
row.note: The commentary makes the rain-fed growth of plants an image for a community's flourishing; in Jesus' parable the earth produces growth beyond the sower's understanding, adding the hidden process between sowing and harvest.

row.basis: one plants, another waters, God gives growth
row.note: The commentary turns plants joined together into people who urge one another; Paul describes distinct workers planting and watering within one field, while God supplies the growth.

row.basis: generous sowing yields a generous harvest
row.note: The commentary links righteous deeds and harvest; Paul applies sowing and reaping to generosity, making shared giving the deed that determines the yield.

row.basis: seed for sowing and a growing harvest of righteousness
row.note: The commentary joins good works to a crop image; Paul says God supplies seed and increases the harvest of righteousness, explicitly making ethical fruit the result.

row.basis: plowman and thresher hope to share the crop
row.note: The commentary says produce has a due and pasture nourishes animals; Paul interprets the crop law as giving field workers hope of sharing the harvest, making labor and entitlement explicit.

row.basis: reaper gathers fruit for life and sower and reaper rejoice together
row.note: The commentary pictures a community made fruitful through linked action; Jesus describes harvest workers rejoicing together as fruit is gathered, giving shared labor and shared outcome a concrete scene.

row.basis: one sows while another reaps
row.note: The commentary connects mutual exhortation with plants joined into continuous growth; Jesus' saying assigns sowing and reaping to different people, making cooperation across roles explicit.

row.basis: reaping what others labored to sow
row.note: The commentary's green community is formed through reciprocal action; Jesus says his hearers enter work others began, adding continuity across generations of sowers and reapers.

row.basis: fig tree given another year and extra care
row.note: The commentary joins patience to the crop's fate; the gardener asks for another year to dig and fertilize a fruitless fig tree, making patience an intervention that could change the harvest.

row.basis: fruit determines whether the tree is spared or cut down
row.note: The commentary contrasts productive greenery with crop loss; the gardener's final condition is that the tree bear fruit or be cut down, making the outcome hinge on yield.

row.basis: weeds burned while wheat is gathered
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the fruitful exception from a lost harvest; Jesus' harvest separates wheat for storage from weeds for burning, adding a final sorting of productive and useless growth.

row.basis: rain falls on just and unjust alike
row.note: The commentary's cloud releases rain onto a community while its later image distinguishes the righteous exception; Jesus says rain falls on both just and unjust, adding an account of weather as an indiscriminate gift.

row.basis: hail and fire burn trees and green grass
row.note: The commentary's fire-bearing whirlwind burns a garden; Revelation's first trumpet sends hail and fire onto the earth, burning trees and green grass in an apocalyptic destruction scene.

row.basis: one person sharpens another
row.note: The commentary interprets connected plants as people who counsel one another; Proverbs gives mutual sharpening as a concrete image of how one person forms another, though it does not use agricultural imagery.

row.basis: good deeds have fruit in this world and a principal kept for the next
row.note: The commentary exempts people who believe, do good, and counsel one another; Peah lists kindness and peacemaking among deeds whose fruit is enjoyed now while their principal remains for the world to come, giving the ethical exception a rabbinic account of reward.
